---
title: "Federated similarity search"
---

```{python}
#| include: false
import os

os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "2")
```

## The use case

A clinician has an unusual case and wants to ask a network of hospitals
whether anyone has seen patients like it. Each hospital holds
embeddings of its own patients, produced by a model it fine-tuned
privately. Nobody will share embeddings, and nobody will share a model.

There are two obstacles, and only one of them is cryptographic.

The **geometric** obstacle: embeddings from different fine-tunes do not
live in a shared space. An inner product between a query from the
public base model and a hospital's privately fine-tuned embedding is
not a similarity — it is a comparison between two different coordinate
systems.

The **cryptographic** obstacle: the query must not be readable by any
hospital, the databases must not be readable by anyone, and no single
party may be able to decrypt.

## The adapter

Each site fixes the geometry locally. A public *anchor cohort* is
published; each site embeds it with its own fine-tuned model, and then
fits the orthogonal map that best carries the public geometry onto its
own. That map is the site's **compatibility adapter**, and it never
leaves the site.

Orthogonality is doing real work here. An orthogonal map preserves
inner products, so moving the query into a site's coordinates leaves
the similarity unchanged. A general linear map would stretch some
directions and shrink others, and the number that came back would no
longer be a cosine.

The direction also matters, and it is easy to get backwards: the
adapter is applied to the *incoming query*, so it must map public
coordinates to site coordinates. The database stays where it is.

## The synthetic network

Three sites, each with its own fine-tune and its own small cohort. The
drift is drawn as an exactly orthogonal matrix, which matters for what
comes next: it means the orthogonal adapter can undo it *exactly*, so
the comparison at the end can assert equality rather than settle for a
tolerance. The [sweeps](#does-the-adapter-have-to-be-orthogonal) later
on this page relax that.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from homomorphepy.examples.similarity import DGP, simulate

anchor_public, sites = simulate()
p = DGP["p"]

pd.DataFrame({
    "site":     [s["name"] for s in sites],
    "patients": [len(s["database"]) for s in sites],
    "drift is orthogonal to": [
        f"{np.max(np.abs(s['drift'].T @ s['drift'] - np.eye(p))):.1e}"
        for s in sites
    ],
})
```

The public anchor cohort is `{python} anchor_public.shape[0]` embeddings
of width `{python} p`. Every site embeds those same anchors with its own
model, which is the only thing the sites hold in common.

## The adapters

Each site fits its own adapter and keeps it. Fitting is a Procrustes
problem — the orthogonal $A$ minimizing
$\lVert A Z_{\text{public}}^\top - Z_{\text{site}}^\top\rVert$ — solved
by an SVD, entirely locally and in the clear.

```{python}
from homomorphepy.examples.similarity import fit_adapter

for s in sites:
    s["adapter"] = fit_adapter(anchor_public, s["anchor_site"])
    # The adapter should reproduce the site's own anchor embeddings
    # from the public ones.
    s["anchor_error"] = float(np.max(np.abs(
        s["adapter"] @ anchor_public.T - s["anchor_site"].T
    )))

[f"{s['anchor_error']:.1e}" for s in sites]
```

Reconstruction to floating-point noise, as promised — the drift is
orthogonal and an orthogonal map inverts it exactly.

## Threshold keys, and rotation keys without a secret key

The querier's vector is encrypted under a joint public key that no
single party can invert.

```{python}
from homomorphepy import fhe_context, ThresholdSite, make_threshold_master
from homomorphepy.examples.similarity import CKKS_PARAMS

ctx = fhe_context("CKKS", **CKKS_PARAMS)
holders = [ThresholdSite(s["name"], None, lambda d, t: 0.0) for s in sites]
master = make_threshold_master("Aggregator", ctx, holders)
CKKS_PARAMS
```

Everything on this page needs one more kind of key. Both operations
below are built from **rotations** of an encrypted vector's slots, and a
rotation needs an evaluation key of its own.

In the ordinary single-key setting those are derived from the secret
key. Under threshold keys there is no secret key to derive them from —
that is the entire point — so they are built by an $n$-of-$n$ ceremony
mirroring the one that produced the public key. Each site contributes a
share of every rotation key in turn:

```{python}
from homomorphepy.actors import make_joint_rotation_keys

make_joint_rotation_keys(master, range(1, p))
```

That is `{python} p - 1` rotation amounts, each requiring a pass around
all three sites. It happens once, at setup.

```{python}
from homomorphepy import Ct

# A round trip through one rotation, to show the keys work: rotating by
# k brings slot k into slot 0.
ct_probe = master.encrypt(np.arange(p, dtype=float).tolist())
ct_rot = Ct(ctx.cc.EvalRotate(ct_probe.raw, 3), ctx.cc)
round(float(np.asarray(master.decrypt(ct_rot, length=p), dtype=float)[0]), 6)
```

## Applying the adapter under encryption

A matrix times an *encrypted* vector cannot be written as a matrix
product — there is no encrypted vector to index into. It can be written
using the matrix's generalized diagonals, $d_i[j] = A[j, (j+i) \bmod p]$:

$$A\,q \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} d_i \odot \mathrm{rot}(q, i).$$

Every term multiplies the encrypted vector by an *unencrypted* diagonal.
That is much cheaper than multiplying two encrypted quantities, and
because the diagonals never need encrypting the whole product costs a
single level of the precision budget.

```{python}
from homomorphepy.examples.similarity import diagonals

def matvec(ct, diags, master):
    """A q, for encrypted q and an unencrypted A given as diagonals."""
    cc, codec = master.ctx.cc, master.codec
    total = None
    for i, d in enumerate(diags):
        if not np.any(d):                       # a zero diagonal adds nothing
            continue
        rot = ct if i == 0 else Ct(cc.EvalRotate(ct.raw, i), cc)
        term = Ct(cc.EvalMult(rot.raw, codec.encode(d.tolist())), cc)
        total = term if total is None else Ct(cc.EvalAdd(total.raw, term.raw), cc)
    return total
```

Check it against the cleartext product on a real query:

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(20260914)
query = rng.normal(size=p)
query /= np.linalg.norm(query)

ct_query = master.encrypt(query.tolist())
ct_mapped = matvec(ct_query, diagonals(sites[0]["adapter"]), master)

got = np.asarray(master.decrypt(ct_mapped, length=p), dtype=float)
want = sites[0]["adapter"] @ query
float(np.max(np.abs(got - want)))
```

The package ships the same routine, so a page that drifts from the
implementation would show it here as a failed comparison rather than as
prose that quietly stops being true.

## The inner product, and folding the slots

With the query in the site's coordinates, the similarity against one
patient is an inner product. Multiplying slot-wise by that patient's
own unencrypted vector puts the $p$ products in $p$ slots; the sum then
has to be gathered into one slot.

Doing that by $p$ rotations would be wasteful. Repeated
rotate-and-add doubles the stride each step and finishes in
$\log_2 p$ = `{python} int(np.log2(p))` rotations, leaving the total in
every slot — slot 0 included, which is the one we read.

```{python}
def slot_sum(ct, p, cc):
    """Fold every slot into slot 0 in log2(p) rotate-and-add steps."""
    out, step = ct, 1
    while step < p:
        out = Ct(cc.EvalAdd(out.raw, Ct(cc.EvalRotate(out.raw, step), cc).raw), cc)
        step *= 2
    return out

patient = sites[0]["database"][0]
term = Ct(ctx.cc.EvalMult(ct_mapped.raw, master.codec.encode(patient.tolist())),
          ctx.cc)
score = np.asarray(master.decrypt(slot_sum(term, p, ctx.cc), length=p),
                   dtype=float)[0]

float(score), float(want @ patient), abs(float(score) - float(want @ patient))
```

One encrypted score, agreeing with the cleartext inner product, and at
no point did any party hold the query in the clear.

## What each party does

Putting the pieces in their places:

**The querier** encrypts its embedding under the joint public key and
sends it. It learns only the scores that come back.

**Each site** applies its own adapter to the encrypted query with
`matvec`, then runs the slot-wise multiply and `slot_sum` once per
patient. Its adapter and its database stay put; only encrypted scores
leave. Note what it never does: decrypt. It cannot.

**The aggregator** collects the encrypted scores and runs the $n$-of-$n$
decryption ceremony on each, then sorts. It holds no key share.

## The whole protocol

```{python}
from homomorphepy.examples.similarity import run

r = run()
print(f"{r.n_candidates} candidates across 3 sites, embedding width {r.p}")
for name, i, score in r.top_k:
    print(f"  {name} patient {i}: {score:.6f}")
```

Nothing above was decrypted except the final scores, and those only
through the $n$-of-$n$ ceremony. The aggregator saw encrypted values
throughout.

## Does it give the right answer?

The protocol is only worth anything if it returns what the same search
would have returned in the clear.

```{python}
print(f"max score error vs cleartext : {r.max_abs_score_error:.2e}")
print(f"identical ranking            : {r.rank_agreement}")
```

The scores agree to CKKS approximation error, and the ranking — which
is what a user actually consumes — is identical.

## Does the adapter have to be orthogonal?

Everything above runs at the orthogonal endpoint, where the adapter
inverts the drift exactly and the score is a true cosine. But real
fine-tuning is not orthogonal. A site that trains freely stretches some
directions more than others, and no rotation can undo that.

So relax the constraint. Fit the adapter by minimizing

$$\lVert Z_{\text{site}} A - Z_{\text{public}}\rVert^2
  \;+\; \mu \lVert A^\top A - I\rVert^2,$$

where $\mu \to \infty$ forces orthogonality (the Procrustes solution
used above), $\mu = 0$ is unconstrained least squares, and values in
between give near-orthogonal maps.

These sweeps run **in the clear**. The encrypted and unencrypted scores
agree to $10^{-13}$, so running them through encryption would cost
hours and change no digit — and what is being asked here is a
statistical question, not a cryptographic one.

Each point is a federated retrieval over three sites, averaged over
replicates of forty queries, so the whole set takes long enough that it
is recorded once by `docs/_recorded/record_similarity_sweeps.py` rather
than run on every build. The figure below is drawn from that file; no
value is typed into this page.

```{python}
import json
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

rec = json.loads(Path("_recorded/similarity_sweeps.json").read_text())
ample, scarce = rec["mu_ample"], rec["mu_scarce"]
beta_tab = pd.DataFrame(rec["beta_sweep"])

pd.DataFrame(
    {"mu": ample["mu_labels"], "design 1": ample["d1"],
     "design 2": ample["d2"], "||AᵀA − I||": ample["aniso"]}
).round(3)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-sweeps
#| fig-cap: "Adapter behavior across the family. Top left: recall against mu at fixed drift, both deployments, with the no-drift ideal, the no-adapter floor, and the convex Gram alternative. Top right: recall against drift magnitude for three members of the family. Bottom left: the same mu sweep when the calibration cohort is smaller than the embedding dimension. Bottom right: how far the fitted adapter departs from an isometry, which is the budget the raw-database deployment spends."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(len(rec["mu_grid"]))
k = rec["config"]["top_k"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9, 7), constrained_layout=True)

# (1) recall vs mu, both deployments, against the three reference lines
a = ax[0, 0]
a.plot(x, ample["d1"], "o-", color="black", label="Design 1 (fold)")
a.plot(x, ample["d2"], "o--", color="firebrick", mfc="none",
       label="Design 2 (matvec)")
a.axhline(ample["gram"], ls="-.", lw=2, color="orange", label="Gram-PSD")
a.axhline(ample["ideal"], ls=":", color="darkgreen", label="ideal")
a.axhline(ample["unaligned"], ls=":", color="gray", label="unaligned")
a.set(xticks=x, xticklabels=rec["mu_grid"], ylim=(0, 1),
      xlabel="μ  (0 = least squares  →  inf = Procrustes)",
      ylabel=f"recall@{k}", title=f"Recall vs μ (β = {ample['beta']})")
a.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=7, frameon=False, ncols=2)

# (2) recall vs drift magnitude, three members of the family
a = ax[0, 1]
a.plot(beta_tab["beta"], beta_tab["procrustes"], "o-", color="black",
       label="Procrustes (μ = inf)")
a.plot(beta_tab["beta"], beta_tab["near_orthogonal"], "o--", color="blue",
       mfc="none", label="near-orthogonal (μ = 1)")
a.plot(beta_tab["beta"], beta_tab["least_squares"], "^:", color="firebrick",
       mfc="none", label="least squares (μ = 0)")
# Drawn as a curve, not a horizontal line: the no-drift reference is
# recomputed at each beta and moves a little with the draw, so
# flattening it to one number would hide that.
a.plot(beta_tab["beta"], beta_tab["ideal"], ":", color="darkgreen",
       label="ideal")
a.set(ylim=(0, 1), xlabel="β  (non-isometry)", ylabel=f"recall@{k}",
      title="Procrustes vs relaxed adapters")
a.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=7, frameon=False)

# (3) the same sweep under scarce calibration: the sweet spot
a = ax[1, 0]
a.plot(x, scarce["d1"], "o-", color="black", label="Design 1 (fold)")
a.plot(x, scarce["d2"], "o--", color="firebrick", mfc="none",
       label="Design 2 (matvec)")
a.set(xticks=x, xticklabels=rec["mu_grid"], ylim=(0, 1), xlabel="μ",
      ylabel=f"recall@{k}",
      title=f"Scarce anchor (n = {scarce['n_anchor']} < p = {rec['config']['p']})")
a.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=7, frameon=False)

# (4) departure from isometry: the cost Design 2 pays at finite mu
a = ax[1, 1]
a.semilogy(x, np.asarray(ample["aniso"]) + 1e-16, "o-", color="black")
a.set(xticks=x, xticklabels=rec["mu_grid"], xlabel="μ",
      ylabel=r"$\|A^\top A - I\|_F$", title="Departure from isometry")

plt.show()
```

Reproduce with:

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 uv run python docs/_recorded/record_similarity_sweeps.py
```

Three things fall out.

**Alignment is not optional.** Without an adapter, recall collapses to
`{python} round(ample["unaligned"], 3)` against an achievable
`{python} round(ample["ideal"], 3)` — the gray floor in the first
panel. The geometric obstacle is the whole problem; the encryption is
the easy part.

**The two deployments coincide only at the orthogonal endpoint.** At
$\mu = \infty$ the two curves in the first panel meet, exactly as the
algebra says they must: an orthogonal map preserves norms, so folding
it into the database and applying it to the query are the same
operation. At finite $\mu$ they separate, and folding wins — because
the renormalization it performs repairs some of the distortion the
non-orthogonal map introduces. The last panel is the budget being
spent: $\lVert A^\top A - I\rVert_F$ falls to
`{python} f"{ample['aniso'][-1]:.0e}"` at the endpoint and rises by
orders of magnitude as $\mu$ relaxes.

**An intermediate $\mu$ beats both endpoints.** The best point on the
Design 1 curve is $\mu =$
`{python} ample["mu_labels"][int(np.argmax(ample["d1"]))]` rather than
either end. The rigid endpoint gives up recall it does not need to;
unconstrained least squares distorts the geometry more than it repairs.
Neither extreme is the right default, and the third panel shows the
effect sharpening when the calibration cohort is smaller than the
embedding dimension — there the intermediate $\mu$ is regularizing an
adapter that least squares cannot determine.

The second panel varies the drift itself. $\beta$ is the non-isometry
magnitude: $\beta = 0$ is an exactly orthogonal fine-tune, and larger
values stretch directions increasingly unevenly. At $\beta = 0$ the
orthogonal adapter matches the ideal — it inverts an orthogonal drift
perfectly, which is the sanity check that the machinery is right. As
$\beta$ grows the rigid adapter falls away while the relaxed ones hold.
That is the practical finding: **the more freely a site fine-tunes, the
more the orthogonality constraint costs you**, and a deployment facing
genuinely free fine-tuning should not default to Procrustes.

The convex Gram alternative sits in the first panel for comparison. It
is analytic and therefore attractive, and it lands at
`{python} round(ample["gram"], 3)` — essentially the no-alignment
floor. Its rotation invariance is exactly the problem: it discards the
orientation of the public frame, which is the one thing a public query
needs.

## What this does not do

**Top-$k$ selection happens in the clear.** The aggregator decrypts
every candidate score and then sorts. Selecting the top $k$ *under*
encryption is possible in CKKS via polynomial sign approximation, but
it costs depth and complexity out of proportion to what it adds here.
The consequence is that the aggregator learns every score, not only the
$k$ it returns.

**Patient indices travel in the clear** alongside the encrypted scores,
so the aggregator learns which site holds a match and at which local
position, though not who that patient is.

**Repeated adaptive queries leak.** A querier who submits many chosen
embeddings learns about the shape of the cohort. That is a property of
any retrieval system that returns real answers, and encryption does not
address it; query budgets do.

**The trust model is honest-but-curious.** A site that misreports its
scores can corrupt the ranking undetected. Catching that needs
verifiable computation, which this does not attempt.

**One encrypted value per patient.** At this scale that is fine. A
production deployment would pack many patients into the slots of a
single encrypted value and amortize both the adapter and the reduction
across them.
